title: Titration Curve Comparison
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: AP Chemistry
description: Side by side Chart.js titration curves for 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl and 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. Curves are calculated from the charge balance; the equivalence point, buffer region, half-equivalence point, and indicator ranges are marked, and a slider compares the pH in both flasks at the same volume.

learningObjectives: Compare titration curves for strong acid-strong base and weak acid-strong base titrations
Identify the equivalence point, half-equivalence point, and buffer region on a titration curve
Explain differences in curve shape and choose a suitable indicator
standards: AP Chemistry CED Unit 8, Topic 8.5: Acid-Base Titrations

controls.label: NaOH added
controls.description: Volume of 0.100 M NaOH added, 0 to 50 mL in steps of 0.1; moves a marker along both curves

controls.label: Show Both on One Chart
controls.description: Toggles between side by side charts and a single overlay chart

controls.label: Tooltip
controls.description: Hovering over a curve shows the volume and pH at that point

equations: Weak acid: [H+] + [Na+] = [OH-] + [A-], with [A-] = C x Ka / (Ka + [H+])

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Side by side comparison with a shared probe
keyQuestions: Why do both acids reach the equivalence point at the same volume of base?
Why is the pH at the weak acid's equivalence point above 7?
Why do the two curves coincide after the equivalence point?
commonMisconceptions: Believing the equivalence point always occurs at pH 7
Believing a weak acid needs less base to neutralize than a strong acid of the same concentration
Confusing the half-equivalence point with the equivalence point
assessmentOpportunities: Have students tabulate the pH of both flasks at key volumes and explain the largest differences
